title: Claude Evaluation and Observability
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to define evaluation criteria for Claude, assemble representative test cases, and use recorded production observations to identify regressions. After completing it, learners can turn a loosely stated quality goal into a repeatable evaluation workflow.
objectives: Define measurable success criteria for a Claude use case.
Create representative test cases that include normal, difficult, and unacceptable outcomes.
Select human review, rule-based grading, model-based grading, or a documented combination for each criterion.
Connect production observations to an evaluation set without treating isolated examples as conclusive.
Compare a proposed change with a baseline and make a documented release decision.

sections.title: Source correction
paragraphs: The source record supplied for the prior module pointed to the module's own catalogue path, named an unregistered publisher, and had never been verified. That record was replaced with two official Anthropic documentation pages: one on defining success criteria and one on developing test cases.

This correction affects source attribution and review currency. It does not change the module's instructional scope: defining success, constructing evaluations, examining observed behavior, and comparing changes with a baseline.
sections.callout: The previous catalogue path was not retained as a source because it was not a resolvable HTTPS reference from an authoritative publisher.

sections.title: Level and prior knowledge
paragraphs: This is an intermediate module. It assumes basic experience writing prompts for Claude and manually reviewing responses. It does not assume prior experience with formal evaluation systems or observability infrastructure.

In this module, an evaluation is a repeatable process that applies stated criteria to test cases. Observability means retaining permitted evidence about actual behavior, such as the input context, output, outcome, error state, and timing, so that failures can be investigated and useful cases can be added to later evaluations.

sections.title: Define success before testing
paragraphs: Begin with the behavior the application must produce, not with a preferred prompt. Convert broad goals such as good quality into criteria that a reviewer or grader can apply consistently. A criterion should identify the behavior being judged, the evidence used to judge it, and the condition that counts as acceptable.

Separate criteria when they represent different risks. Factual correctness, instruction following, appropriate refusal, output structure, and response time may require different evidence and grading methods. Record which criteria are mandatory and which are preferences before comparing alternatives.

Choose a grading method for each criterion. Human review is useful when judgment depends on context or nuance. Rule-based grading is useful when a requirement can be checked directly. Model-based grading can help scale qualitative review, but its instructions and outputs must also be validated against examples reviewed by people.
sections.callout: Do not define success after seeing the candidate results. Doing so makes the comparison easier to bias.

sections.title: Build representative test cases
paragraphs: A test case contains an input, any relevant context, and the expected behavior or grading criteria. Include ordinary cases that reflect the intended use, difficult cases near known boundaries, and cases representing outcomes the application must avoid.

Use realistic variation rather than repeating one template. Vary phrasing, context length, ambiguity, and other conditions that matter to the use case. Keep a separate set of cases for final comparison when repeatedly revising prompts against a development set, because repeated exposure can make performance on familiar cases look more general than it is.

When a production failure reveals a distinct and relevant behavior, remove or transform sensitive information as required, document why the case matters, and add an appropriate version to the evaluation set. Preserve the original criterion unless the product requirement itself has changed.

sections.title: Connect observations to evaluation
paragraphs: Evaluation asks whether behavior meets predefined criteria. Observability supplies evidence about what happened during actual use. The two practices reinforce each other: evaluation detects known failure patterns before release, while observed failures can reveal missing cases or criteria.

For each permitted record, retain enough context to reproduce or classify the outcome. Useful categories can include the use-case identifier, input characteristics, output, grader result, human-review result, error state, and timing. Record only information the application is authorized to retain, and apply the application's privacy and retention requirements.

Do not treat one successful example as proof of general quality or one failure as proof that every similar case will fail. Classify the observation, find related test cases, and run the relevant evaluation before drawing a broader conclusion.

sections.title: Compare changes with a baseline
paragraphs: Run the same evaluation set and grading criteria against the existing baseline and the proposed change. Compare results by criterion and by meaningful case category, not only as one combined result. A combined result can conceal a serious regression in a smaller but important category.

Investigate disagreements between grading methods. If a rule passes a response that human reviewers reject, determine whether the rule, the criterion, or the response is at fault. Document any grading change and rerun the affected comparison so that the baseline and candidate remain comparable.

Make the release decision using the acceptance conditions defined before testing. Save the evaluation inputs, criteria, grading instructions, results, and decision rationale that policy permits. This creates a reviewable link between the proposed change, the observed evidence, and the decision.
sections.callout: A repeatable evaluation workflow consists of predefined criteria, representative cases, documented grading, a stable comparison, and a recorded decision.

questions.prompt: When should acceptance criteria be defined for a comparison?
choices: After reviewing the candidate results
Before comparing the baseline and candidate
Only after a production failure
Whenever the preferred candidate performs poorly
questions.explanation: The module says to define success and acceptance conditions before comparing alternatives so that observed results do not bias the criteria.

questions.prompt: Which test set best follows the module's guidance?
choices: Many copies of one easy prompt
Only cases on which the current prompt succeeds
Ordinary, difficult, and unacceptable-outcome cases with realistic variation
A single production example selected after release
questions.explanation: Representative evaluation requires ordinary cases, difficult boundary cases, unacceptable outcomes, and realistic variation.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended response to a distinct and relevant production failure?
choices: Treat it as proof that all similar requests fail
Ignore it because it was not in the original evaluation
Replace every existing test case with the failure
Classify it, protect sensitive information, and add an appropriate version to the evaluation set
questions.explanation: The module directs learners to classify observed failures, apply privacy requirements, and turn relevant failures into evaluation cases.

questions.prompt: Why should results be compared by criterion and meaningful case category?
choices: A combined result can hide a serious regression in a smaller category
Categories eliminate the need for predefined criteria
Category results make a baseline unnecessary
Every category must use a different prompt
questions.explanation: The module warns that one combined result can conceal regressions affecting a smaller but important category.

questions.prompt: What should happen when a rule-based grade passes a response that human reviewers reject?
choices: Discard the human reviews automatically
Release the candidate because the rule passed
Investigate the disagreement, document any grading change, and rerun the affected comparison
Change the acceptance criteria without recording the change
questions.explanation: Disagreements must be investigated, and any grading change must be documented and applied to a rerun so the comparison remains valid.
